summary: Defines how to use the Password-Based Message Authentication Code 1 (PBMAC1) from RFC 8018 inside PKCS #12 files, amending RFC 7292 and RFC 8018. It allows more modern password-based key derivation functions and supports regulatory compliance. It was replaced by RFC 9879.

eli5.summary: A PKCS #12 file is a locked box of keys. This allows a newer, stronger way to seal it with a password. It has been replaced by RFC 9879.

questions: how do you protect pkcs 12 with a password
why is pbkdf2 better than the original pkcs12 kdf
subtitle: Using modern key derivation with password-based integrity protection in PKCS #12 files.

tldr.problem: PKCS #12 files protect keys and certificates with a password, but the original key derivation function was weak and limited. PBMAC1 from RFC 8018 offers stronger derivation methods like PBKDF2 and scrypt, and better flexibility for regulatory compliance.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC specifies how to embed PBMAC1 (Password-Based Message Authentication Code 1) into the PKCS #12 MacData structure, allowing the use of modern key derivation functions while maintaining backward compatibility with legacy tools.
tldr.outcome: PKCS #12 files can now use stronger password-based protection and support regulatory requirements. However, it was superseded by RFC 9879.

today: RFC 9579 is Informational and updates RFCs 7292 and 8018. It has been superseded by RFC 9879, which provides updated guidance on password-based integrity protection in PKCS #12.

sections.title: Overview of PKCS #12
sections.content:
The PKCS #12 format is widely used to package certificates, private keys, and secrets in a portable way that can be moved between applications and machines. The format protects this sensitive material with password-based integrity protection: the contents are scrambled using a password.

Unfortunately, RFC 7292 mandates a specific key derivation function that was designed to be simple but offers limited flexibility. It can only change the underlying message digest function, not the derivation method itself. This RFC extends PKCS #12 to allow PBMAC1, a more flexible password-based authentication mechanism that supports modern key derivation functions like PBKDF2 and scrypt.
sections.eli5: PKCS #12 is a password-protected box for keys. The old way of locking it was weak. This adds a stronger lock that modern systems prefer.

sections.title: Why Better Key Derivation Matters
sections.content:
Key derivation functions turn a password into a cryptographic key. The original PKCS #12 method had security concerns and was not extensible. PBKDF2, specified in RFC 8018, applies a hash function many times to slow down attackers. scrypt, from RFC 7914, is even more resistant to brute-force attacks by using more memory.

Regulatory compliance in some jurisdictions requires the use of specific key derivation functions like PBKDF2. The new syntax allows applications to choose PBKDF2, scrypt, or future methods without changing the overall PKCS #12 structure. Legacy applications that cannot interpret PBMAC1 can still decrypt the key material, provided they ignore MAC verification failures.
sections.eli5: Modern password methods are better at stopping attackers who guess passwords. Some countries require them. The update lets PKCS #12 use these stronger methods.

sections.title: Embedding PBMAC1 in PKCS #12
sections.content:
The PKCS #12 MacData structure contains a digest algorithm identifier. This RFC permits the id-PBMAC1 object identifier as a valid algorithm type. When PBMAC1 is used, the parameters field MUST contain PBMAC1-specific parameters.

The macSalt and iterations fields of the MacData structure are ignored when PBMAC1 is used. The actual salt and iteration count come from the PBMAC1 parameters instead. For backward compatibility, these fields SHOULD NOT be empty or zero, even though they are ignored.
sections.eli5: PKCS #12 files have a standard format. This change adds a new algorithm option (PBMAC1) that takes its own parameters for the password derivation.

sections.title: Recommended Algorithms and Parameters
sections.content:
All implementations MUST support PBKDF2 paired with SHA-256 HMAC for both integrity check and the pseudorandom function (PRF). The key length generated by the KDF MUST be explicitly encoded in the parameters and SHOULD match the HMAC output size, typically 32 octets for SHA-256.

When using PBKDF2, implementations MUST include the keyLength field in the PBKDF2-params and MUST NOT accept PBKDF2 without it. Implementations SHOULD NOT use PBKDF2 with SHA-1 HMAC due to its age. Hash functions with 160 bits or less MUST NOT be used. Implementations MAY support SHA-3 or scrypt for additional flexibility.
sections.eli5: To work with other systems, all implementations must support SHA-256 with PBKDF2. Weaker hash functions are not allowed. Newer methods like SHA-3 are optional but welcome.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
PBMAC1 and PBKDF2 security inherit from RFC 8018, so all security considerations from that document apply. The main risk is that KDF parameters are not cryptographically protected; an attacker with access to the file could modify the iteration count or salt.

To mitigate this, implementations MAY refuse to process KDF parameters that specify very small key output sizes (less than 20 octets), which would be vulnerable to brute-force attacks on the HMAC. It is RECOMMENDED to reject any parameters specifying less than 20 octets.
sections.eli5: The security depends on the strength of the password and the derivation method. Weak passwords can still be guessed. Very small key sizes are dangerous.
